https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text: The road to Kostyantynivka covered with anti-drone nets. The road to Konstyantynivka in Donetsk, Ukraine, is a perilous journey for the Khyzhak brigade – a mobile unit tasked with shooting down Russian drones to cover soldiers’ rotations or moving armoured vehicles By Julia Kochetova Mon 24 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 02.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “Holy yeah! Yeaaaah! Done!” Booooooom. “Easy peasy lemon squeezy!” Dzhango from the Khyzhak brigade shouts in English. He has just shot down a Russian FPV drone. View image in fullscreen Dzhango firing to shoot down a Russian FPV-drone. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Russian waiting drone after being shot on the road by a mobile firing crew View image in fullscreen Dzhango, a shooter, gets ready before the daily shift View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Dzhango loads a magazine while brushing his teeth in the dugout before the daily shift. Inside the dugout of the mobile firing crew of Khyzhak brigade View image in fullscreen Young and Dzhango taking a break after the shift. A small moving target that wants to kill you is a challenge with an asterisk. I don’t manage to photograph the drone above us, but I’m glad that Dzhango shoots more accurately. The normal rule is for everyone else is to stay under cover and not stick your head out. View image in fullscreen The remains of burned vehicles on the road View image in fullscreen A ground robot returning from a logistic mission The tasks of Dzhango’s mobile fire group are different – to stand watch and shoot down Russian drones. The H20 highway runs from the frontline city of Kramatorsk to the battlefield in Kostyantynivka in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region. The last road always becomes either the “road of life” or the “road of death”. Drone warfare is deadly simple – everything flies toward the road; any movement is a target. Us too. View image in fullscreen The moon over the road The road is covered with scars: FPV drones, cluster munitions, artillery, glide bombs – a map of modern war. Pears on the ground are entangled with fibre-optic cable – this harvest will not be gathered. Anti-drone nets fall on to a highway strewn with burned-out ground robots, pickup trucks, and armoured vehicles. Donetsk is crumbling before my eyes. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen A Russian fibre optic drone flies above the mobile firing crew. Dzhango loads a magazine during the shift The fighters of the Khyzhak brigade are police patrol officers who joined up. The five of them share a dugout with Zhuzha, a dog that came to them in search of food and cuddles. A shower, a washbasin, a kitchen, even a plasma TV playing Michael Jackson’s They Don’t Care About Us – a parallel universe built underground. The peace sign on Jackson’s T-shirt contrasts with the sound of loading magazines. View image in fullscreen The mobile firing unit of Khyzhak brigade on duty View image in fullscreen Soldiers from Khyzhak brigade fire on a Russian drone during the rotation. Borya, a shooter on duty View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Soldiers stop for a quick chat – they use scooters to drive between positions Above, the kill zone, which lives by its own rules: food and water are delivered by ground robots, via electric scooters, or through the sky while Ukrainian Vampire drones carry supply packages above. “We try as much as possible to shoot down whatever is flying toward us. We understand that it’s someone’s ground robot, or someone’s car, or even – someone’s life,” Dzhango tells me. He is 31, from Chernivtsi, which is more than 1,000km away. View image in fullscreen Dzhango and Young during a shift View image in fullscreen Dzhango near the ruins of a home In the morning he talks to his family on a video call – on the screen there’s a beach, white sand, colourful umbrellas, his son – a parallel world. “What I miss most is my family, my child … living through the coolest moments of his childhood from a distance. His first baby teeth fell out! And I wanted to pull them out with a string, as my father did.” His son knows exactly what Dzhango’s job looks like and asks: “Bring me an FPV!” Dzhango does not bring FPVs home. His son’s birthday is tattooed on his right arm. On the left – a long scar and a tattoo: “Jump off the cliff and wings will grow.” It is a reminder of his father’s advice and of a police shift in Chernivtsi, when he was wounded – three bullets – and his 22-year-old colleague, Taisiia Tataryn, was killed. After a long rehabilitation, he joined the combat unit. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Young and Dzhango pass a burned-out scooter. A soldier was injured while driving on it and evacuated from the combat area. Fibre optic cable mixed with pears on the ground in Donetsk region View image in fullscreen Remains of a shot-down Russian FPV Every morning we walk the same streets and tree lines, but the landscape changes – fresh craters, fallen trees, smoke on the horizon. The remains of drones and munitions form a map of the area – here a Molniya, a Russian kamikaze drone, is stuck in a tree. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen The body of a civilian covered with plastic sheeting near the road to Kostyantynivka. The body of a Ukrainian soldier – which was evacuated a few days later Here – since the beginning of July – a dead civilian has been lying under a black plastic bag. A little further on – a soldier from a neighbouring unit, his body will be evacuated in a couple of days. In the tree line – a burned scooter, an FPV strike; a fighter from another unit was evacuated, but the soldiers will say that he died in hospital that night. View image in fullscreen Soldiers driving on a buggy at high speed, risking being spotted by a drone “Something’s flying!” – within seconds the guys start shooting. Dzhango’s comrade, 41-year-old Young, associates every successful shoot-down with adrenaline and a rush. He served almost eight years in the police and almost two years in the Khyzhak brigade. View image in fullscreen Young, a shooter from Khyzhak brigade, on duty with the mobile firing crew View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Young collecting apricots next to the road. Young taking a break On his very first combat mission, two small fragments entered his body; he calls it luck. On the next one – an FPV drone hit the side window of his armoured vehicle – the shaped charge flew inside. “A flash behind me – out of the corner of my eye I see that something exploded inside. Sparks, smoke, you can’t see anything, it’s impossible to breathe,” he recalls. View image in fullscreen One of his brothers-in-arms died instantly; a second was seriously wounded: “I guess the shaped charge passed through him, and then hit the floor where another fighter was sitting … And it exploded between his legs.” Now his task is to make sure another FPV does not reach his comrades’ vehicle. The only intact building among the erased skeletons of houses is the church. View image in fullscreen Dzhango lighting a candle in a damaged church View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Holy images inside the damaged church near the road to Kostyantynivka A blue eye looks out. Some of the saints are on the floor, others remain by the altar. Dzhango lights a candle – according to tradition, a candle is lit either for the health of the living or for the repose of those no longer here. Half an hour later, the artillery shelling will begin, and the church will come under fire. A week later I receive a short message: “The church burned down.” While waiting for the rotation out, we sit along the highway on scattered chairs and stools under the dense cover of the trees. View image in fullscreen Tsygan from Khyzhak brigade is driving soldiers for rotation on the road towards Kostyantynivka, Donetsk region View image in fullscreen Soldiers from Khyzhak brigade after the rotation Dzhango plays Madonna’s Music from his phone, then Justin Timberlake’s Mirrors, and dances a little. From time to time he pauses – to stop and listen whether something is flying. Then he turns the music back on and sings along again. Even in abnormal circumstances, inside war – at least you can always choose the soundtrack. View image in fullscreen The road to Kostyantynivka covered with anti-drone nets View image in fullscreen A sunset over the road to Kostyantynivka The next day Dzhango will write saying that they shot down another nine drones. And then – send a video of how another morning in the dugout began with “Good Morning, good morning to you” from the musical Singin’ in the Rain. “Easy peasy lemon squeezy!”, he said. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/19.text: Listen (2 mins) Save Share Ukrainian suspect, a ‘trained scuba diver’, arrested over Nord Stream blast on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google In this photo from November 28, 2025, police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor, after Italy's top court approved the handover to Germany of the Ukrainian man suspected of coordinating the Nord Stream gas pipeline blasts [Thilo Schmuelgen/Reuters] By Reuters and The Associated Press Published On 19 Aug 2026 19 Aug 2026 A second Ukrainian suspect alleged to have been involved in the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline blasts has been arrested in Croatia and will be extradited to Germany, German prosecutors said on Wednesday. The German government welcomed the arrest of the man, identified as Vladimir Z, on Wednesday. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 ‘A stress test’: US-Germany rift widens as Iran war drags on list 2 of 4 Who is Gerhard Schroeder, Putin’s pick for Ukraine peace talks mediation? list 3 of 4 What is the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline that Russia, China are planning? list 4 of 4 German prosecutors allege Ukraine ordered Nord Stream pipeline attack end of list “We’re simply glad that the federal prosecutor’s office is making progress in these investigations, because it’s important that the bombing of the pipelines be clarified as well,” Ministry of Justice spokesman Nicholas Limmer told reporters in Berlin. The first suspect in the case, former Ukrainian army officer Serhii K, was charged by prosecutors in July with orchestrating the blasts while acting on behalf of Ukrainian state entities. The Ukrainian national, who was arrested in Italy in August 2025 and transferred to Germany in November, has denied any involvement in the blasts near the Danish island of Bornholm. Authorities in Kyiv have said they did not have enough information to respond in detail to the German allegations. Germany’s federal prosecutors’ office said Vladimir Z was arrested in the Croatian city of Pula by local police forces acting on a European arrest warrant. The prosecutors said he was a trained scuba diver who was part of a group led by Serhii K that planted explosives targeting the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines. Russia and Western countries have described the September 2022 explosions, which followed Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine earlier that year, as sabotage. Advertisement The explosions damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, a vital route for Russian gas exports to Europe, as well as the Nord Stream 2 branch, which had yet to enter service. At the time, Moscow had recently halted gas deliveries via Nord Stream 1, blaming Western sanctions and technical issues, though Europe accused it of weaponising energy supplies. Poland has long opposed the Nord Stream pipelines, viewing them as an attempt by Russia to use its vast energy resources to gain leverage across Europe. German prosecutors have said the aim of the alleged attack was to permanently halt gas deliveries through the pipelines and thereby prevent Russia from using revenue from the natural gas trade to finance its war effort. German courts have treated the case as falling within their jurisdiction because the damaged pipelines end in the German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and their loss affected Germany’s energy security and internal safety.

https://www.thevermilion.com/what-will-t.text: What will these military exercises of the Volunteers for Ukraine be like (in which Italy does not want to participate) The willing accelerate their support for Kiev, driven above all by Andy Burnham. At the Coalition meeting, coinciding with the anniversary of Ukrainian independence, the British Prime Minister authorizes the provision of confidential plans for … Written by: Jack Williams Published on: August 26, 2026 The willing accelerate their support for Kiev, driven above all by Andy Burnham. At the Coalition meeting, coinciding with the anniversary of Ukrainian independence, the British Prime Minister authorizes the provision of confidential plans for the Storm Shadow long-range missile to allow the French and Ukrainians to accelerate production of the long-range weapon in Ukraine. On the same day, French President Macron announced that the “Multinational Force for Ukraine” exercises will be conducted in October and November. What should we expect They will not simply be tanks firing blanks on a firing range, much less a direct threat to Russia. The large military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing will have one objective above all: to test in advance how to bring a European military force to Ukraine in case the war with Russia ends. The joint maneuvers – unofficially over 25 nations would have joined the coalition – will have to demonstrate the “operational readiness” of the armies and the ability to act once hostilities have ceased. Italy, according to what has been made known by government sources, will not participate, consistently with the line maintained so far by Giorgia Meloni: support for Ukraine especially on the negotiating level, but no Italian soldiers on Ukrainian territory. The force that should enter Ukraine after the war To understand what the “Willing” will practice doing, we need to start from the Multinational Force for Ukraine, the Mnf-U. It is not a NATO force and it is not even a UN blue helmet mission. It is a military structure created within the coalition led mainly by the United Kingdom and France to provide Ukraine with security guarantees after a possible ceasefire. The plan is already much more advanced than a simple political declaration. The force has been declared “Ready to Operate”, i.e. organizationally ready to come into operation. Its operational headquarters is in Paris and since 24 July command has passed to British General Tom Bateman, supported by a French deputy commander. London claims that over 25 nations are participating in the project, although a list of contingents has not been published nor has it been clarified how many soldiers each country would be willing to deploy. The condition is basic: this force should not enter Ukraine while the current war is underway. The Coalition documents provide for its deployment, at Kiev’s request, only after a “credible cessation of hostilities”. The tests begin in Poland A first piece of the exercise has already been defined. Poland will host the first Coalition military maneuvers. Donald Tusk’s government has announced that British and French forces will take part, along with Polish soldiers and other allied units. And we also know what one of the main exercises will be. Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Bejda announced the arrival of around 1,500 British and French soldiers starting in September. He defined them as “logistical-transport” exercises, aimed in particular at preparing the rapid transfer of troops. Put more simply: the armies will test the route that could one day bring men and equipment from Western Europe towards the Ukrainian border and, if political order arrives, into Ukraine. It means organizing rail and road convoys, transporting heavy vehicles, fuel and equipment, coordinating armies that speak different languages ​​and use different systems, setting up communications and common commands and ensuring the protection of columns during movements. Poland, in this scheme, would inevitably become one of the great logistical hubs of the future mission. Warsaw has also announced the preparation of infrastructures that allow a more stable presence on its territory of allied forces in addition to the US forces already present. What would European soldiers do in Ukraine The Mnf-U would have two tasks that the British define as “regeneration and reassurance”. The first is to continually replenish Ukrainian military capacity: train soldiers, provide equipment, organize supplies, and help Kiev maintain an army strong enough to deter a second Russian attack. The second concerns the actual Western military presence. The plans include land, air and sea capabilities. London also spoke of patrols in the skies and seas intended to create the conditions for the recovery of civil aviation, investments and the Ukrainian economy. This does not necessarily mean deploying thousands of European soldiers in the trenches of Donbass. On the contrary, the logic of the mission would be to operate mainly in the rear, in training centers, in logistics hubs, in bases and in the protection of air and maritime space. And it is exactly this device that the autumn exercises will have to begin to put to the test. Because Italy said no Italy continues to be part of the Coalition of the Willing and Giorgia Meloni also participated in the last meeting. Rome also continues to support Kiev militarily and financially. But the government has long drawn a red line on the presence of Italian soldiers. After Macron’s announcement, government sources specified that Italy will not participate in the exercises, explicitly recalling the “no to Italian soldiers” in Ukraine. The decision is significant because these maneuvers are not intended as a NATO exercise to defend an Alliance country. They serve specifically to prepare the force that may be called upon to operate on Ukrainian territory. Participating in it would therefore mean entering directly into the military preparation of that future mission. The problem: what happens if Russia attacks again? It is also why these exercises have political importance far greater than the number of soldiers involved. The ultimate goal of the MNF-U is to create deterrence. After a hypothetical agreement, Moscow should know that a new attack on Ukraine could mean hitting not only Ukrainian soldiers, but also British, French or other European countries. And this is where the risk of the project lies. The multinational force would not automatically be a NATO mission. A possible Russian attack against European soldiers located on Ukrainian territory would therefore not automatically equate to the activation of Article 5 of the Atlantic Alliance. The answer would depend on the security guarantees agreed with Kiev and the decisions of individual governments. But this very possibility should represent the deterrent: forcing the Kremlin to consider that a new offensive could turn into a direct clash with some European armies. The maneuvers of October and November therefore serve to answer a very concrete question: if a ceasefire were signed tomorrow, how quickly would Europe really be able to transform the promises made to Ukraine into soldiers, planes, ships and vehicles deployed on the ground? Beállítom Karácsony Gergely főpolgármester szerint a főváros jelenlegi pénzügyi helyzete a jogtipró jellegű állami pénzelvonás miatt alakult ki, de heteken belül megállapodás születhet a városvezetés és a kormány közt a helyzet rendezéséről. A Fővárosi Közgyűlés pénteki ülésén Karácsony napirend előtti felszólalva azt mondta, hogy az előző kormány okozta bajt a jelenlegi kormányzatnak és a fővárosnak kell közösen orvosolnia – írta az MTI. A tárgyalások miniszteri és főpolgármesteri szinten indultak el, jelenleg pedig helyettes államtitkári, illetve szakértői szinten zajlanak, és előrehaladott állapotban vannak, mondta a főpolgármester. Kiemelte, reményeik szerint a majdani megállapodás biztosítani fogja, hogy a következő években ne ismétlődjenek meg, illetve ne termelődjenek újra a jelenlegi pénzügyi problémák. Karácsony szerint az Orbán-kormány sok százmilliárd forintot vett el a fővárostól törvénytelenül, de az ehhez vezető lépésekről az Alkotmánybíróság is kimondta, hogy az Alaptörvénybe ütköztek. A főpolgármester reménykeltőnek nevezte a Fővárosi Közfejlesztések Tanácsának (FKT) újraindítását, az Európai uniós forrásokról pedig úgy fogalmazott, hogy nagyon komoly fejlesztési időszak előtt állunk, mert rengeteg forrás érkezik közlekedésfejlesztésre és köztéri megújításra, illetve reméli, hogy a lakhatást érintő felhívások is megjelenhetnek. Orbán Árpád, a Tisza Párt fővárosi frakciójának vezetője szerint Magyarország és Budapest előtt hatalmas lehetőségek állnak. „Ehhez dolgozni kell. Nem csak a parlamentben, nem csak a kormánynak, nem csak a miniszterelnöknek és a minisztereinek. Nem várhatunk mindig külső segítséget” – mondta. Hozzátette: slágertéma, hogy a főváros csődben van. „Remélem, utoljára halljuk, nem kifogáskeresés kell.” Orbán Árpád szerint a kormány és az Országgyűlés munkájának köszönhetően történelmi léptékű forrásokhoz jut a főváros. A közbiztonsági és köztisztasági helyzettel kapcsolatban a fővárosi és a kerületi önkormányzatok vezetőinek felelősségét hangsúlyozta a Tisza fővárosi frakcióvezetője, mert szerinte ez sem kizárólag a kormány, a Belügyminisztérium feladata. http://www.heraldglobe.com/news/27931460.text: Trump hails 'major progress' on setting up US Army base in Poland RT.com 18 Sep 2026, 09:11 GMT+10 The president made the announcement as Russia warned European NATO members against provoking a war with Moscow The US has made major progress in negotiations to establish a military base in Poland, President Donald Trump has announced. His remarks came as Russia warned that it would retaliate if the territory of Poland or the Baltic states were used for a NATO attack against the country. Poland, which borders Russia's Kaliningrad exclave to the northeast, is a key logistics hub for delivering Western military aid to Ukraine and one of Kiev's main supporters in Europe. "GREAT NEWS! Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. "If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance," he added. Nawrocki responded by promising to find "the best possible location" for the base. "We are ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation: seriously, responsibly, and always together," he wrote on X. The US already maintains a permanent Army garrison and command headquarters in Poland, although most of the roughly 10,000 American troops stationed in the country serve on a rotational basis. During Trump's first term, Poland offered in 2018 to host a permanent base tentatively named "Fort Trump." Under Trump's successor, President Joe Biden, the US established a garrison headquartered at Camp Kosciuszko in Poznan and permanently stationed the V Corps Forward Headquarters in the city. Tensions between Russia and NATO have flared in recent months as eastern members of the US-led military bloc have blamed Russia for drone incursions. Moscow has dismissed the allegations as unfounded. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said during a trip to Kiev over the weekend that "if Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly." Russian presidential aide and former security chief Nikolay Patrushev responded to Sikorski by warning that "Polish statehood would cease to exist within two or three days" should a conflict break out. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated this week that the country had no intention of attacking NATO members, but said that if the bloc attacked Russia, the war would be "very short." https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqg7.text: Image source, Getty Images By Paul Kirby ,Â Europe digital editor, Â and Â Alys Davies Published 1 October 2026 Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad to have come under direct attack. The Russian president insisted that Moscow was "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders that it was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030. Throughout this week, Russia has accused Nato of preparing to blockade its territory, which borders Lithuania and Poland, warning that it would even be prepared to use nuclear weapons if the West tried to cut off Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia. Nato has sought to calm the situation, stressing that it was a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to stop its "nuclear threats". Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months. Last week alone, Poland said a Russian helicopter had strayed into its territory adjacent to Kaliningrad and Lithuania said its population felt "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes. Rosenberg: Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine Published 1 day ago In a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin told his audience that he believed that international conflicts were highly likely to continue, but would get better as "Western hegemony" weakened. Although the Russian leader himself began the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, he again blamed the West for provoking the invasion, arguing that Moscow had simply been forced to defend itself and take up arms. He also insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea. "Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," he said. Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war. Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since the war in Ukraine started in 2022. Other civilian infrastructure is also regularly hit, with a key bridge in Kyiv attacked by drones on Thursday. Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts. "If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said. He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea that he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear. "We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that." He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled. Western officials have long feared that, rather than invading Kaliningrad, Russia would use the relatively small distance between the exclave and ally Belarus - known as the Suwalki Gap - were it to attempt to seize Lithuanian territory by force. Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC last week that his country had made evacuation plans in case Russia invaded and thousands of Nato troops are stationed there. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and that the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful". Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said that unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used. He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly be fired at the end. He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence. "The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said.
